name: Thymulin

lead: Thymulin is a nine-amino-acid hormone made by the thymus that needs zinc to be active. It appears in peptide and zinc discussions as an immune and general-health option, not as a cosmetic one.

The chain runs from a zinc-dependent thymic hormone to immune regulation to general health. It was described by Jean-Francois Bach and colleagues in 1977 and has been studied for T-cell differentiation, neuroendocrine regulation and inflammation. Human data cover zinc status and thymic function, not supplement use.

paras: Some vendors sell it as a research peptide in longevity circles; users often pair the idea with attention to zinc intake.
No human safety trials of the peptide were found. It is not an approved drug and is sold unregulated.

angle.text: Thymulin is a thymus hormone that needs zinc to be active, discussed in peptide and zinc circles for immune and general health. Human data covers zinc status and thymic function; appearance has not been studied.

lead: Thymulin, also called facteur thymique sérique (FTS) or serum thymic factor, is a nine-amino-acid peptide (pGlu-Ala-Lys-Ser-Gln-Gly-Gly-Ser-Asn) produced by the thymus and requiring zinc for biological activity [1][1]. It was described by Jean-Francois Bach and colleagues in 1977 [1].

Research has concerned its role in T-cell differentiation, neuroendocrine regulation and inflammation [1][2]. It is sold by some vendors as a research peptide in longevity circles, but no human trials of thymulin as a treatment were found, and it has no recognized appearance use.

paras: Thymulin is thought to help T-cell differentiation and to enhance T and NK cell activity. Its secretion follows a circadian rhythm and is linked to the hypothalamic-pituitary axis [1][3]. Levels decline with age, and it appears to dampen inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha in part by inhibiting NF-kB signaling [1].

Zinc dependence was shown in 1982, when metals were found to contribute to the activity of serum thymic factor [4]. A 1988 study found that serum thymulin activity fell in mildly zinc-deficient volunteers and recovered after zinc supplementation [5].

No studies found of thymulin as a treatment. The human data that exist concern zinc status and circulating thymulin activity [5]; an analog peptide has been examined in animal models of pain and neuroinflammation [1].
Thymulin is sold as a research peptide and is not an approved drug. Its link to looksmaxxing is indirect, through longevity and immune-support claims; no appearance outcomes have been studied.
